title: Discrete-Time Signals
description: Describe, transform and classify sequences: impulses and steps, shifts and reversals, periodicity, exponentials and energy.

study.title: Sequences, impulses and steps
study.body: A discrete-time signal $x[n]$ is a list of numbers indexed by an integer $n$, drawn as a stem plot; between the integers it is simply not defined. The unit impulse $\delta[n]$ is 1 at $n = 0$ and 0 elsewhere, the unit step $u[n]$ is 1 for $n \geq 0$. The impulse is the first difference of the step, $\delta[n] = u[n] - u[n-1]$, and multiplying by a shifted impulse picks out one sample (**sifting**). The plot shows the pulse $u[n] - u[n-4]$: four samples, $n = 0 \ldots 3$.

study.title: Explore: shift and reversal
study.body: $x[n-n_0]$ is $x[n]$ delayed (moved right) by $n_0$ samples; $x[n+n_0]$ is advanced. $x[-n]$ mirrors the sequence about $n = 0$. For $y[n] = x[n_0 - n]$, reverse first and then shift right by $n_0$: sample $x[0]$ lands at $n = n_0$. Drag $n_0$: grey is $x[n]$, coloured is $x[n_0 - n]$.

study.title: Time scaling and amplitude changes
study.body: $y[n] = x[2n]$ keeps only the even-indexed samples (decimation or downsampling): the odd samples are lost for good, so this is not reversible. $y[n] = x[n/2]$ is only defined for even $n$; the gaps are filled with zeros (or interpolated), which stretches the sequence (upsampling). Amplitude transformations act on the values instead: $A\,x[n] + B$ scales and offsets every sample. Grey: $x[n]$, coloured: $x[2n]$.

study.title: Even and odd parts
study.body: Every sequence is the sum of an even part ($x_e[-n] = x_e[n]$) and an odd part $x_o[n] = \tfrac{1}{2}(x[n] - x[-n])$, with $x_o[-n] = -x_o[n]$. The odd part is always 0 at $n = 0$ and its samples add up to zero, so the sum (and the average value) of $x[n]$ sits entirely in the even part. Products follow sign rules: even × even and odd × odd are even, even × odd is odd.

study.title: Periodic sequences
study.body: $x[n]$ is periodic if $x[n+N] = x[n]$ for some integer $N$; the smallest such $N$ is the fundamental period. A DT sinusoid $\cos(\Omega_0 n)$ is periodic only if $\Omega_0 / 2\pi$ is a ratio of integers $k/N$ (in lowest terms): then $N$ samples span exactly $k$ cycles. $\cos(3\pi n/8)$ has $\Omega_0/2\pi = 3/16$, so $N = 16$ (3 cycles); $\cos(0.5n)$ is not periodic at all.

study.title: Explore: frequency repeats every 2π
study.body: Because $n$ is an integer, $\cos((\Omega + 2\pi)n) = \cos(\Omega n)$: only $0 \leq \Omega \leq \pi$ gives distinct sinusoids. The fastest possible oscillation is $\Omega = \pi$, $\cos(\pi n) = (-1)^n$. Drag past $\pi$: the samples (dots) slow down again and lie on the orange $\cos((2\pi - \Omega)n)$. For a sampled signal $x[n] = x(nT)$, the DT frequency is $\Omega = \omega T$ rad/sample.

study.title: Explore: exponentials, energy and power
study.body: $a^n u[n]$ decays for $|a| < 1$, grows for $|a| > 1$ and alternates in sign when $a < 0$. Energy $E = \sum |x[n]|^2$; a decaying exponential has finite energy, $E = 1/(1 - a^2)$. Periodic sequences have infinite energy but finite average power $P$ (the average of $|x[n]|^2$ over one period), e.g. $A^2/2$ for $A\cos(\Omega_0 n)$ ($0 < \Omega_0 < \pi$). The complex exponential $e^{j\Omega n} = \cos\Omega n + j \sin\Omega n$ has $|x[n]| = 1$, so $P = 1$.

steps.title: Sequences and stem plots
steps.body: A discrete-time signal is a sequence of numbers $x[n]$ with integer index $n$. Most come from sampling: $x[n] = x(nT)$ with sample period $T$. We draw them as stem plots. This one is $x[-1] = 2$, $x[0] = 1$, $x[1] = -1$, $x[2] = 3$ and zero elsewhere; written with impulses it is $2\delta[n+1] + \delta[n] - \delta[n-1] + 3\delta[n-2]$.

steps.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \left(n^2 + {{c}}\right)\delta[n - n_0]$ for $n_0$ = {{n0}}.
steps.explanation: Sifting: $\delta[n - n_0]$ is nonzero only at $n = n_0$, so the sum picks out one sample of $n^2 + {{c}}$: $({{n0}})^2 + {{c}}$ = {{n0^2 + c}}.

steps.title: Impulses and steps
steps.body: The step is the running sum of the impulse, and the impulse is the first difference of the step: $\delta[n] = u[n] - u[n-1]$. A difference of two steps gives a rectangular pulse: $u[n - a] - u[n - b]$ switches on at $n = a$ and off again **at** $n = b$, so its last nonzero sample is $n = b - 1$ and it has $b - a$ samples.

steps.prompt: Which expression describes the sequence in the graph?
steps.explanation: The pulse starts at $n$ = {{a}} and its last sample is at $n$ = {{b-1}} ({{L}} samples). $u[n-{{a}}]$ switches on at $n$ = {{a}}; subtracting $u[n-{{b}}]$ switches it off from $n$ = {{b}} on. $u[n+{{a}}] - u[n+{{b}}]$ is not even positive: it equals $-1$ for $-{{b}} \leq n \leq {{-a-1}}$.

steps.title: Shifting and reversing
steps.body: $x[n - n_0]$ moves the sequence $n_0$ samples to the **right** (a delay), $x[-n]$ mirrors it about $n = 0$. Combined, $x[n_0 - n]$: first reverse, then shift the mirrored sequence right by $n_0$. Check one sample: $x[0]$ ends up where $n_0 - n = 0$, at $n = n_0$. Drag $n_0$ to try it.

steps.prompt: $x[n]$ is nonzero only for ${{N1}} \leq n \leq {{N2}}$. Consider $y[n] = x[{{a}} - n]$.

ask.prompt: What is the **lowest** $n$ for which $y[n]$ can be nonzero?
ask.explanation: $y[n] = x[{{a}} - n]$ is nonzero when ${{N1}} \leq {{a}} - n \leq {{N2}}$, i.e. ${{a-N2}} \leq n \leq {{a-N1}}$. The lowest index is {{a-N2}}: the **last** sample of $x$ becomes the **first** of $y$.

ask.prompt: What is the **highest** $n$ for which $y[n]$ can be nonzero?
ask.explanation: $y[n] = x[{{a}} - n]$ is nonzero when ${{N1}} \leq {{a}} - n \leq {{N2}}$, i.e. ${{a-N2}} \leq n \leq {{a-N1}}$. The highest index is {{a-N1}}: the **first** sample of $x$ becomes the **last** of $y$.

steps.prompt: $y[n] = x[2n]$ still contains every sample of $x[n]$, just squeezed closer together.
steps.explanation: $y[0] = x[0]$, $y[1] = x[2]$, $y[2] = x[4]$, … The odd-indexed samples $x[1], x[3], \ldots$ never appear: decimation throws information away, unlike time compression of a continuous signal.

steps.prompt: Match each transformation to what it does.
steps.explanation: Changes inside the brackets act on the time index: $n - 3$ delays, $n + 3$ advances, $-n$ mirrors, $2n$ decimates. Changes outside act on the sample values.

steps.prompt: How many nonzero samples does $x[n] = u[n+{{N1}}] - u[n-{{N2}}]$ have?
steps.explanation: $u[n+{{N1}}]$ switches on at $n = -{{N1}}$, $u[n-{{N2}}]$ switches off at $n$ = {{N2}}. The nonzero samples are $n = -{{N1}} \ldots {{N2-1}}$: {{N1}} + {{N2}} = {{N1+N2}} samples.

steps.prompt: The samples $x[0] \ldots x[4]$ are {{x0}}, {{x1}}, {{x2}}, {{x3}}, {{x4}}; all other samples are 0. Find $y[{{n0}}]$ for $y[n] = {{A}}\,x[{{a}} - n] + {{B}}$.
The samples $x[0] \ldots x[4]$ are {{x0}}, {{x1}}, {{x2}}, {{x3}}, {{x4}}; all other samples are 0.

ask.prompt: Find $y[{{j}}]$ for the decimated sequence $y[n] = x[2n]$.
$y[n] = x[n/2]$ for even $n$ and 0 for odd $n$ (upsampling). Find $y[{{2*j}}]$.
$y[n] = x[n/2]$ for even $n$ and 0 for odd $n$ (upsampling). Find $y[{{2*j+1}}]$.
ask.explanation: $n$ = {{2*j+1}} is odd, so $n/2$ is not an integer and $y[{{2*j+1}}]$ = 0 by definition: the zeros fill the gaps between the stretched samples.

steps.prompt: $x[-2] \ldots x[2]$ are {{xm2}}, {{xm1}}, {{xz}}, {{xp1}}, {{xp2}}; all other samples are 0.

ask.explanation: $x_e[0] = \frac{1}{2}(x[0] + x[0]) = x[0]$ = {{xz}}. The odd part is always 0 at $n = 0$.

steps.prompt: The graph shows $x[n]$. Which graph shows $y[n] = x[2 - n]$? (Grey numbers: $n$ of the first and last nonzero sample.)
steps.explanation: Evaluate a few samples: $y[1] = x[1] = 1$, $y[0] = x[2] = 3$, $y[-1] = x[3] = 2$. So the mirror image $x[-n]$ (samples at $n = -3 \ldots -1$) is shifted **right** by 2, to $n = -1 \ldots 1$. $x[-2-n]$ would shift it left, $x[n-2]$ is only a delay without reversal, and $x[-n]$ is the plain mirror image.

steps.prompt: If $x[n]$ is odd, the sum of all its samples is zero.
steps.explanation: For an odd sequence $x[-n] = -x[n]$, so the samples at $n$ and $-n$ cancel in pairs, and $x[0] = -x[0]$ forces $x[0] = 0$. The sum of a sequence lives entirely in its even part.

steps.prompt: Match each item to its result.
steps.explanation: Adding and subtracting $x[-n]$ separates the parts. For products: $(-1)\cdot(-1) = +1$, so odd × odd is even; even × odd changes sign under $n \to -n$, so it is odd.

steps.prompt: All samples $x[0] \ldots x[{{L-1}}]$ are nonzero and all others are zero. How many nonzero samples does $y[n] = x[{{k}}n]$ have?
steps.explanation: $y[n] = x[{{k}}n]$ is nonzero when $0 \leq {{k}}n \leq {{L-1}}$, so $n = 0 \ldots {{floor((L-1)/k)}}$: {{floor((L-1)/k)+1}} samples. The other {{L-floor((L-1)/k)-1}} samples of $x$ are discarded.

steps.prompt: Find the fundamental period $N$ (in samples).

ask.explanation: $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{{{p}}}{2 \cdot {{q}}} = \frac{{{p}}}{{{2*q}}}$, already in lowest terms. So $N$ = {{2*q}} samples, which contain $k$ = {{p}} cycles. ($2\pi/\Omega_0$ = {{2*q/p}} is not an integer, so it is not the period.)

$\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{{{p}}}{{{q}}}$, already in lowest terms. So $N$ = {{q}} samples, which contain $k$ = {{p}} cycles. ($2\pi/\Omega_0$ = {{q/p}} is not an integer, so it is not the period.)

steps.prompt: Which of these sequences is **not** periodic?
steps.explanation: $\cos(2n)$ has $\Omega_0/2\pi = 1/\pi$, which is irrational: no integer $N$ makes $2N$ a multiple of $2\pi$. The others have $\Omega_0/2\pi$ = 1/10, 3/14, 1/4 and 1/2, with periods 10, 14, 4 and 2.

steps.prompt: $x(t) = \cos(2\pi f_0 t)$ with $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}} is sampled at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}, giving $x[n] = \cos(\Omega_0 n)$.

ask.prompt: After how many samples does $x[n]$ repeat?
ask.explanation: $\Omega_0/2\pi = f_0/f_s$ = 1/{{fs/f0}}, so $N$ = {{fs/f0}} samples: one period of $x(t)$ contains exactly {{fs/f0}} samples.

steps.prompt: $x[n] = \cos({{r}}\pi n)$ produces exactly the same samples as $\cos(\Omega n)$ with $0 \leq \Omega \leq \pi$. Find $\Omega$.
steps.explanation: Subtract $2\pi$ (no change for integer $n$) and use that cosine is even: $\cos({{r}}\pi n)$ $= \cos(({{r}} - 2)\pi n)$ $= \cos({{2-r}}\pi n)$. So $\Omega$ = {{2-r}}π = {{(2-r)*pi|rad}}.

steps.prompt: Set $\Omega$ so that $\cos(\Omega n)$ repeats every {{N}} samples with exactly **one** cycle per period.
steps.explanation: One cycle in $N$ samples means $\Omega N = 2\pi$: $\Omega = 2\pi/{{N}}$ = {{2*pi/N|rad}}, i.e. $\Omega/\pi$ = {{2/N}}. The dots at $n = 0$ and $n$ = {{N}} are then both at the peak.

steps.prompt: Find the energy of $x[n] = {{A}}\,({{a}})^n\,u[n]$.
steps.explanation: $E = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} A^2 (a^2)^n = \frac{A^2}{1 - a^2}$ (a geometric series with ratio $a^2$ = {{a^2}}). $E = \frac{{{A^2}}}{1 - {{a^2}}}$ = {{A^2/(1-a^2)}}. The sign of $a$ does not matter for the energy.

steps.prompt: A periodic sequence repeats the four samples {{v0}}, {{v1}}, {{v2}}, {{v3}} forever. Find its average power.
steps.explanation: For a periodic sequence, average over one period: $P$ $= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |x[n]|^2$ $= \frac{1}{4}({{v0^2}} + {{v1^2}} + {{v2^2}} + {{v3^2}})$ = {{(v0^2+v1^2+v2^2+v3^2)/4}}. The energy is infinite, the power is finite: a power signal.

steps.prompt: Which stem plot shows $x[n] = (-{{a}})^n\,u[n]$?
steps.explanation: $|-{{a}}| < 1$, so the magnitude decays as {{a}}$^n$; the negative base flips the sign every sample. The other graphs show {{a}}$^n$ (no alternation) and the growing sequences with $|a| = 1/{{a}} > 1$.

steps.prompt: The samples $x[0] \ldots x[4]$ are {{x0}}, {{x1}}, {{x2}}, {{x3}}, {{x4}}; all other samples are 0. Let $y[n] = x[{{a}} - 2n]$.

ask.prompt: How many samples of $y[n]$ can be nonzero?
ask.explanation: $y[n]$ uses $x[{{a}} - 2n]$, and the index ${{a}} - 2n$ always has the parity of {{a}}. Only indices 0 … 4 hold samples, so $y$ picks up {{3-mod(a,2)}} of them: $x[0], x[2], x[4]$ for an even shift, $x[1], x[3]$ for an odd one.

steps.prompt: Find the fundamental period of $x[n] = \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{{{N1}}}\right) + \sin\left(\frac{2\pi n}{{{N2}}}\right)$.
steps.explanation: The terms have periods {{N1}} and {{N2}}. The sum repeats when both do: at the least common multiple, $N$ $= \frac{{{N1}} \cdot {{N2}}}{\gcd({{N1}}, {{N2}})}$ $= \frac{{{N1*N2}}}{{{g}}}$ = {{Nl}} samples.

steps.prompt: $x(t) = \cos(2\pi f_0 t)$ with $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}} is sampled at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: After how many samples does $x[n]$ repeat (its fundamental period $N$)?
ask.explanation: $\frac{\Omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{f_0}{f_s} = \frac{{{a}}}{{{b}}}$. Dividing by $\gcd({{a}}, {{b}})$ = {{g}} gives lowest terms $\frac{{{a/g}}}{{{b/g}}}$, so $N$ = {{b/g}} samples.

ask.prompt: How many periods of $x(t)$ fit in one period of $x[n]$?
ask.explanation: $\frac{f_0}{f_s} = \frac{{{a}}}{{{b}}}$, or $\frac{{{a/g}}}{{{b/g}}}$ in lowest terms (divide by $\gcd$ = {{g}}): $N$ = {{b/g}} samples span $k$ = {{a/g}} periods of the analog cosine ({{b/g}} × {{1/fs|s}} = {{a/g}} × {{1/f0|s}}).

steps.prompt: Find the average power of $x[n] = {{B}} + {{A}}\cos(\pi n/{{q}})$.
steps.explanation: Square: $B^2 + 2AB\cos(\Omega_0 n) + A^2\cos^2(\Omega_0 n)$. Over one period the cosine averages to 0 and $\cos^2$ to 1/2, so $P = B^2 + A^2/2 = {{B^2}} + {{A^2/2}}$ = {{B^2+A^2/2}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps to build $y[n] = x[3 - 2n]$ from $x[n]$ in order.
steps.explanation: Work from the inside out: each step replaces $n$ in the previous result. Shift first ($n \to n + 3$), then scale ($n \to 2n$), then reverse ($n \to -n$). Checking a few samples directly in $x[3 - 2n]$ confirms the result.

steps.prompt: $x[n] = ({{a}})^n\,u[n]$ has finite energy.
steps.explanation: $E = \sum_{n \geq 0} (a^2)^n$ converges only when $a^2 < 1$, i.e. $|a| < 1$ (then $E = 1/(1 - a^2)$). Here $|a|$ = {{abs(a)}}. For $|a| = 1$ the samples never decay ($E = \infty$ but $P$ is finite).

steps.prompt: $x(t) = \cos(2\pi f_0 t)$ with $f_0$ = {{f0|Hz}} is sampled at {{fs|Hz}} without anti-aliasing filter. Written as $\cos(\Omega n)$ with $0 \leq \Omega \leq \pi$, what is $\Omega$?
steps.explanation: $\Omega = 2\pi f_0/f_s$ = {{2*r}}π, which is above π. Subtract $2\pi$ and use the even symmetry of cosine: $\Omega = 2\pi$ − {{2*r}}π = {{2*(1-r)}}π. The samples look like a sinusoid at {{fs-f0|Hz}}: the alias.
